newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russians protest but vigour less than expected.
newsitem.headline: Russians protest but vigour less than expected.

text.p: Tens of thousands of angry Russians protested against unpaid wages and government policy on Thursday but 11th-hour Kremlin efforts appeared to defuse tensions in the nuclear state of 150 million.

Russian news agencies quoted the Interior Ministry as saying the total number of protesters was likely to be less than two million -- one tenth of that forecast by the trade union organisers, who gave no fresh figures on Thursday afternoon.
There were no reports of violence or disturbances.

The biggest protests were staged in a sunny, frosty Moscow where police put the number of demonstrators at over 80,000 and in St Petersburg, where 40,000 people in the central Palace Square had to contend with heavy snow.
St Petersburg radio said factories started paying wage arrears at 3 p.m. (1200 GMT), just when the speeches started.

The unions, backed by Russia's communist-led opposition, had organised the strikes and demonstrations to protest at wage arrears of over 50 trillion roubles ($8.8 billion), including 10 trillion from the state.
Millions of workers have not been paid for months and cannot afford the goods now crowding the shelves of once-empty shops.

Slogans demanding the resignation of President Boris Yeltsin and his government floated high above many crowds across Russia, accompanied by red flags and portraits of Soviet state founder Vladimir Lenin.
But the dominating mood appeared to be mostly resigned.

"How long will the working people suffer to please the IMF and mafiosi capital?" asked Mikhail Nogaitsev, a senior official with the Moscow trade union organisation. "We need jobs, pensions, wages and social benefits."
Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov told reporters the protest amounted to a no-confidence vote in the cabinet, despite a reshuffle which was completed on Wednesday.
"Changes in the government have convinced no one. This march is going from (the Pacific city of) Vladivostok to Kaliningrad (on the Baltic) and no one can stop it," he told reporters.
But the government's last-minute efforts to quell popular discontent appeared to have partial success.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, in an effort to calm spirits, promised on Wednesday that the state and private employers would pay 11.8 trillion roubles ($2 billion) in back wages and pensions in March.
It was not clear where the money would come from.
Billions of roubles have been dispatched hastily to regions and working groups ahead of the protest.
Yeltsin's spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said the 66-year-old Kremlin leader was following the action closely from his country residence and considered economic demands by the protesters "justified".
The protests are the first test for Russia's new cabinet, named over recent weeks.

Ministers have promised to resolve the crisis as quickly as possible. The new team, led by new first deputy prime ministers Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov has pledged to speed up reforms as the only way out of the crisis.
Many protesters, those who had lost out in six years of turmultous transition to a market economy, had a different view.
"I want to live without shocks and without Yeltsin's therapy," read one banner in Vladivostok, referring to market reforms launched in 1992 and effectively stalled over the last two years.
But the protests were far from universal.
Miners, long Russia's most militant workers and a group hit hard by pay arrears, said they were not striking and were not calling on Yeltsin's government to quit.
The miners, who backed Yeltsin in his early struggles against the communists but dislike many of his current policies, have decided to give the new government a chance.

Firms in the key metals and energy sectors said output would not be affected. Air traffic controllers were not on strike and cosmonauts on the orbiting Mir space station said they were too busy to join the protests.
